title: Why Study AI Safety?
summary: A short motivation for why AI safety matters and I choose to study it.

notes.heading: When did I seriously consider pursuing AI safety?
notes.body:
I started seriously considering AI safety after attending a talk by Yoshua Bengio in 2025. He came to NUS to speak about the risks and safety challenges associated with AI. I already knew that he was a strong advocate for AI safety, but hearing him speak in person affected me deeply.

 He said that he wanted to help ensure a safe world for his children and grandchildren. He had even tried to persuade frontier AI companies to slow down their capabilities research. However, AI development has become a race, and companies are strongly incentivized to be the first to achieve AGI. Wanting to become the best is understandable—it is something that has often been ingrained in us since childhood. But as Professor Bengio pointed out, we need more people working on AI safety because these companies are unlikely to slow down, especially when more capable models can lead to greater profits.

 After completing my PhD, I had the opportunity to work as a postdoctoral researcher at my undergraduate alma mater. Around the same time, I started this website to document my self-learning journey in AI safety. I hope to gradually build genuine expertise in this area, although I do not yet know how long that will take. What I do know is that I eventually want to join an AI safety research team and contribute in a meaningful way.

notes.heading: What problem in AI safety feels personally meaningful to me?
notes.body:
The first problem that deeply intrigues me is model misalignment. In 2025, I read a paper on emergent misalignment, and I became seriously concerned about the issue. I started thinking about how normal it will become for young children to use AI models from an early age, often trusting their advice without yet having the maturity to distinguish what is right from what is wrong.

 I want to help ensure that these risks are properly addressed. More specifically, I want to understand what causes misalignment and whether it can be prevented at a deeper level, rather than relying only on external guardrails. This will likely be the first AI safety problem that I explore in depth. 

 As models become more capable, they may also become better at bypassing external guardrails. That is why I am especially interested in addressing misalignment from within the model itself. I think of it like raising a child. If we only give a child a long list of strict rules, we cannot possibly anticipate every situation in which the child might misbehave. A clever and harmful friend may eventually find a way to influence the child or help them work around those rules. External restrictions alone may not be enough.

 A more robust approach is to help the child understand what is right and wrong, and why harmful behaviour should be avoided. Similarly, I want to explore whether AI systems can be trained to internalize safe principles, rather than merely being prevented from producing harmful behaviour by a layer of external guardrails.
